what_it_does: A chip (called an SoC, or System-on-a-Chip — a single piece of silicon that contains a processor, memory, and other circuitry all in one) is designed once but used for years, while the software workloads it runs keep changing. A chip that is well-suited for today's AI or video workloads may be a poor match for tomorrow's, but chip designers currently have no standard way to measure how much 'workload drift' their design can handle. Neoscope introduces two measurable quantities — Magnitude (how much the workload has changed) and Disruption (how abruptly it changed) — and classifies chips' exposure into four risk levels from 'Minimal' to 'Volatile.' Armed with these metrics, the framework uses a mathematical planning technique (an integer linear program, which finds the best choice among a huge number of options by expressing everything as inequalities) to identify the chip configuration that stays performant across a projected range of future workloads, without brute-force testing every possible design.
